summary: Describes how the NIST Secure Hash Standard family of algorithms can be used with the built-in cryptographic authentication of OSPF version 2. It updates, but does not replace, the mechanism from RFC 2328. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Routers sending each other directions should be sure the notes come from friends. This document adds stronger secret stamps for those notes, based on modern hash math.

subtitle: How OSPFv2 routers can sign their packets with the SHA family of hash algorithms in HMAC mode.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication only allowed Keyed-MD5, and operators asked to use the NIST Secure Hash Standard algorithms instead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC keeps the RFC 2328 authentication process and adds HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512, with the digest appended to each OSPF packet.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256. The RFC updates RFC 2328 without replacing it, and RFC 7474 later updated this document.

today: RFC 5709 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2328 and has itself been updated by RFC 7474. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Add SHA to OSPFv2
sections.content:
OSPF version 2 already had built-in cryptographic authentication, defined in Appendix D of RFC 2328. That mechanism used Keyed-MD5. RFC 5709 adds the Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA) from the US NIST Secure Hash Standard, used in the Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) mode from NIST FIPS 198.

The RFC says the work was driven by operator requests to use the NIST algorithms instead of being forced to use Keyed-MD5. It updates RFC 2328 but does not deprecate or supersede it, and it applies only to Authentication Type 2, Cryptographic Authentication.
sections.eli5: Routers could already stamp their messages with one kind of secret stamp. Now they can pick from newer, stronger stamps.

sections.title: Background: Authentication in the OSPF Header
sections.content:
Every OSPF packet header has an Authentication Type field and 64 bits of data for the chosen scheme. RFC 2328 defines types 0, 1 and 2. The authentication type and its extra data are configured per interface, or equivalently per network or subnet.

With type 2, all routers on a shared network are configured with a secret key. For each packet the key is used to compute a message digest, a one-way function of the packet and the key, which is appended to the end of the packet. Because the key never crosses the network in the clear, this protects against passive attacks.
sections.eli5: Every router on the same street knows the same secret word. Each note gets a stamp made from the note and the word, and the word itself is never written on the note.

sections.title: Supported Algorithms and Requirements
sections.content:
The valid algorithms for OSPFv2 Cryptographic Authentication become Keyed-MD5, HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. The RFC sets these requirements for implementations:

  • MUST support HMAC-SHA-256.
  • SHOULD support HMAC-SHA-1, and also Keyed-MD5 for backwards compatibility.
  • MAY support HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512.

An implementation MUST let operators configure any algorithm it supports for use with any given KeyID. The algorithm in use is implied by the key, not sent in the packet.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know at least one good stamp, and a few other stamps are optional extras.

sections.title: Generating and Verifying the Digest
sections.content:
The overall process from RFC 2328 Appendix D is unchanged. The sender picks a security association, sets the KeyID, sets the Authentication Type to Cryptographic Authentication, and sets the Authentication Data Length to the hash output length in bytes. For SHA-256 that is 32 bytes. The digest lengths are 20 bytes for SHA-1, 32 for SHA-256, 48 for SHA-384 and 64 for SHA-512. The 32-bit cryptographic sequence number is set as RFC 2328 describes.

The digest is computed in two passes. First the Authentication Trailer is filled with a constant called Apad (the hexadecimal value 0x878FE1F3 repeated L/4 times, so it is as long as the hash). The inner hash is then H(Ko XOR Ipad || packet) and the outer hash is H(Ko XOR Opad || First-Hash). The outer hash becomes the Authentication Data. The key Ko is always L octets long: a longer key is hashed, and a shorter one is padded with zeros.

The receiver follows RFC 2328 verification but uses this computation. It must save the received digest before computing the expected one, then compare. Larger hashes make packets larger on the wire.
sections.eli5: The router mixes the note with the secret word twice in a special recipe and attaches the result. The receiver follows the same recipe and checks that the stamps match.

sections.title: Security Associations and Key Changes
sections.content:
The RFC calls the key information an OSPFv2 Security Association. It holds an 8-bit Key Identifier (KeyID), the authentication algorithm, the key, and four times: Key Start Accept, Key Start Generate, Key Stop Generate and Key Stop Accept. OSPFv2 has no in-band way to create or manage these.

For smooth changeovers, KeyStartAccept SHOULD be earlier than KeyStartGenerate, and KeyStopGenerate SHOULD be earlier than KeyStopAccept. If the last key on an interface expires, the router should notify the network manager and treat the key as having infinite lifetime rather than fall back to no authentication.

Because the KeyID is in each packet, the receiver does not have to try every configured association. This helps against denial-of-service attacks but cannot stop an on-link attacker from sending valid-looking packets with bad digests that force costly computation.
sections.eli5: Each secret word has a name tag, so the receiver knows which word to use. Old and new words overlap for a while so nobody gets confused during a swap.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes published concerns about MD5 and SHA, but says the MD5 concerns are not an attack on Keyed-MD5. It also says some organisations prefer NIST algorithms for local policy reasons.

The mechanism is vulnerable to a replay attack by any on-link node, which could record a packet and replay it when its sequence number is valid again. Ideally each security association would be replaced before a sequence number is reused, but no automated key management had been standardised for OSPF at publication, and the same key was commonly used for very long periods.

Symmetric cryptography cannot show which router sent a packet, only that the sender knew the security association. The RFC says the mechanism need not be perfect, and that IPsec or full digital signatures are alternatives. It also says routing data needs authentication but not privacy.
sections.eli5: A sneaky neighbor could copy an old stamped note and send it again later. Changing the secret word often helps, but back then there was no automatic way to do that.
